text: Executive summary

title: PRAVAH: sparse low-cost sensor placement under uncertain wind
text:
The question
How few low-cost, noisy sensors do we need, and where should they go, to reconstruct and forecast a pollution field when the wind and the emissions are uncertain? Plan 2 (plans/plan-02-identifiability-placement-forecast.yaml) breaks this into: which source combinations a network can actually distinguish (identifiability), whether a longer history can replace sensors, which placement rule is best for which task, and finally sequential forecasting (E08–E11).

title: PRAVAH: sparse low-cost sensor placement under uncertain wind
text:
Where we started: Green (2006)
Our methodological starting point is Kary Green’s Rice master’s thesis on optimal sensor placement for parameter identification (Green 2006). Green linearises sensor readings around the parameters of a semi-discretised PDE, forms the Fisher information matrix M = GᵀR⁻¹G, and chooses sensor locations that maximise log det M (D-optimal design). His worked example is a 1-D advection–diffusion problem with two unknown parameters (diffusivity and advection coefficient); the optimised design shrinks the 95 % confidence-ellipse area by about 36 % relative to equal spacing (reading notes, docs/research/green-2006-reading-notes.md).
PRAVAH keeps the Fisher/D-optimal machinery but changes almost everything around it:

title: PRAVAH: sparse low-cost sensor placement under uncertain wind
text:
The testbed
A FiPy finite-volume solver of ∂c/∂t + u·∇c = ∇·(K∇c) − λ(c − c_bg) + S, with K = 50 m² s⁻¹, λ = 1/12 h, Gaussian area sources (σ = 400 m), background 5 µg m⁻³, hourly-piecewise wind, a 60-day calendar split into train (days 1–30), validation (31–42) and test (43–60) with held-out test wind regimes. Sensors sit on a 16 × 16 candidate lattice with 1.25 km minimum spacing. Every experiment received an independent audit (“gate”).

text:
Results at a glance
Evidence labels: verified = engineering check passed an independent gate; exploratory = smoke scale and/or settings chosen after seeing data; confirmatory (cells run) = preregistered test, supported only in the cells run.



Exp
Question
What we did
What we found
Evidence




E00
Can we fix endpoints and rules before data?
Preregistered protocol, evaluation contract; audit
Audit found 3 blockers: signal 1000× below noise (B1), no approval (B2), upwind numerics (B3). All resolved: amendment A1, user approval, amendment A2
approved baseline, amendable


E01
Does the solver solve the PDE?
Convergence, mass, dt-halving oracles 16²–64²
Upwind converges at ~1st order, mass to ~1e-14, but at 64² its numerical diffusivity is 350–2900 m² s⁻¹ vs K = 50. Split VanLeer at dt 30 s gives K_eff ≈ 50 (A2)
verified (conditionally cleared)


E02
Is the benchmark sound and leak-free?
Generator, splits, 65 validity/leakage checks
Checks pass; at 100 µg/s the plume was invisible (SNR ~2e-3); at 1 g/s peak SNR is 21–32
verified (smoke)


E03
Can fixed sensors recover source strengths?
NNLS inverse, 648 fits, 24 h window
Rank-deficient in all 648 fits, at both scales: a structural failure of fixed, non-optimised sensors
exploratory (negative)


E04
Which source combinations can a network distinguish?
Footprints, Fisher information, SVD
At 1 g/s a D-optimal 4-sensor design has practical rank 4/4; coverage 1–2, redundant 2. One replicate
exploratory


E05
Can a longer window replace sensors?
Window × sensors × wind ablation, 20 seeds
Elapsed time alone adds nothing (constant wind); wind change adds rank (+0.37, 16/17 seeds). v1 claims were overstated and withdrawn
exploratory


E06
Can we reproduce standard placement algorithms?
uniform/random/coverage/source-near/D/A/diversity/POD-QR
Implementations check out (QR = PySensors). Source-informed designs reach full rank; most of that is knowing source locations
verified methods; results in-sample


E07
Which placement is best for which held-out task?
32² pilot + 64² sweep (40 scenarios, held-out winds)
D-opt beats random on held-out forecast RMSE by a median 42–84 % per cell (8/8 cells), and under every estimator tried. Which strategy wins depends on estimator memory: near-source beats D-opt with a 24 h window (115/120 pairs), D-opt wins with all past data (103/120)
confirmatory in cells run; strategy ordering exploratory


E08
How many sensors are enough?
Preregistered factorial; 32² pilot; 64² sweep (60 scenarios)
Location-aware designs need k ≈ K sensors; random layouts need 8–16. More sensors beat more readings for random networks, but not once sources are covered. H1, H3, H4 and H5 supported; H2 contradicted. With all past data, 2 sensors suffice for every strategy and H5 reverses
64²: preregistered tests (windowed estimator); not yet audited


E09
Does sequential filtering help?
Kalman filters with independent tests; 32² replay; audit
Estimating sources from all past data cuts forecast error 58–74 % vs a 24 h window. The gain is memory, not filtering. A field-only filter is nearly useless
exploratory, audited


E10
Do drifting-source filters help?
Random-walk augmented filter; constant, diurnal and log-random-walk truths; audit
Constant sources: all past data is best. Time-varying: 1 h error falls 24–55 %, but the filter is 12–15 % worse at 6 h under a diurnal cycle. Calibrated only when q matches the truth
exploratory, audited


E11
Placement optimised for forecasting?
Data-free forecast-variance objective, wind-robust prior; audit
64² (20 clusters): under a 24 h window, beats D-optimal even with an out-of-sample prior (+0.34 at k = 8, 19/20) but loses to near-source. Worse than D-optimal with all past data
exploratory; pilot audited


E12
What do wind errors do?
Biased direction, speed, timing and noise in the inverse wind
Direction ≥ 30° or a lag ≥ 2 h destroys forecast skill. Wrong strengths absorb wind errors while the fit stays good. The memory benefit vanishes
exploratory pilot


E13
What do background, source or sensor errors do?
18 mismatches, with and without an estimated background
Background offset: fixable. Common-mode sensor bias: a silent failure. Wrong source shapes or locations: unfixable. Outages: benign
exploratory pilot


E14
Can the method flag its own failures?
8 truth-free diagnostics; ROC by stress
Moderate at best (AUC 0.71). Speed errors and common sensor bias are undetectable; a missing source is flagged by informed networks but not random ones
exploratory pilot


E15
Do scenario-robust networks hold up better?
Mean/CVaR/worst-case placement over wind ensembles; tail over 18 wind-error conditions
Tail gain indistinguishable from chance. Robust ≈ near-source with a 24 h window; no gain with all past data
exploratory pilot


E16
Do conclusions survive other physics?
One-at-a-time ablations: diffusion, loss, source shape and spacing, background
No reversal. D-opt > random and the memory gain are robust. The memory flip holds in every cell. Some margins weaken
exploratory pilot (32²)


E17
Do the conclusions survive real winds?
Synthetic tracer under ERA5 winds near Belauri; 64², 3 cases × 20 clusters
Placement still beats random (35–64 %). D-optimal vs near-source mostly ties. Only all-past-data forecasts beat the persistence bound. A single-site wind instead of the box mean cancels every advantage (a transport floor)
exploratory, audited; not validation


E18
Can real monitors validate it?
Audit of public PM2.5 data near Belauri
Not conducted: only 2 stations within 100 km, short records; a passive tracer cannot be validated against PM2.5
gap assessment

title: PRAVAH: sparse low-cost sensor placement under uncertain wind
section: What we learned, in plain language
text:
What we learned, in plain language

Scale matters before cleverness. At the originally declared emission rate, sensors could not see the plumes at all; no placement rule can fix that (E00–E05, amendment A1).
Numerics matter. The first-order scheme smeared plumes with 7–60× the physical diffusivity at 64²; switching to a split VanLeer scheme was necessary before any 64² result could mean anything (A2).
Time helps only when the wind changes. Repeated readings under the same wind reduce noise but do not separate sources; a change in wind direction does (E05, exploratory).
Optimised placement beats random, confirmed in the 8 cells run (E07).
Which placement wins depends on how much history the estimator uses. With a 24 h estimation window, sensors next to the known sources beat D-optimal (115/120), because D-optimal networks go blind when an unseen southerly wind blows: 79 % of their error falls in those windows. When the estimator uses all past data, the blind spells are bridged and D-optimal wins (103/120) (E07 + gate-09, exploratory).
Memory matters more than the algorithm. Estimating the persistent sources from all past data cuts forecast error by 58–74 % against a 24 h window; a filter that corrects only the field does almost nothing (E09, exploratory).
Drifting sources need drifting estimates, but only for short horizons. A filter that lets strengths drift helps 1 h forecasts when sources really change, and hurts 6 h forecasts under a daily cycle (E10).
Placement tuned for one estimator loses under another. Forecast-optimised networks win only with a 24 h window, and part of their gain was in-sample (E11).
Model errors dominate placement differences. Under a 30° wind error, a 2 h timing lag or a wrong source map, no estimator beats an oracle persistence bound. Strategies stop mattering. Some of these errors stay hidden in the residuals (speed errors, common sensor bias) (E12–E13).
Self-diagnosis is limited. Truth-free checks catch some failures (timing and direction errors, correlated noise) but not speed errors, a common sensor bias, or (for random networks) a missing source (E13–E14).

title: PRAVAH: sparse low-cost sensor placement under uncertain wind
text:
Honest limitations

Synthetic, perfect-model world: known source locations, known wind, constant sources, ideal sensors, uniform wind.
Smoke scale (32²) for E02–E06; only E07 ran at 64² and only for K ∈ {2, 4}, k ∈ {4, 8, 16}, 10 seeds.
The source scale (1 g/s) was chosen after seeing data, so E02–E06 at that scale are exploratory.
The E07 mechanism rests on one unseen wind direction; the “source-near” advantage may partly reflect sensors sitting inside the 1200 m emission disc. Across all 40 scenarios, excluding those sites keeps near-source ahead (104/120) but shrinks D-optimal’s gain over random from 71 % to 20 %, and no single cell then clears the 10 % test threshold (exploratory control).
E09–E14 are 32² pilots with an upwind surrogate and 6 independent clusters. Their 64² runs are documented but deferred (E11’s is running).

title: 1  Background and starting literature
text:
1.1 Green (2006): the starting point
This chapter says what PRAVAH borrows, from whom, and what it does differently. It is a map, not a review: no paper listed here has been reproduced by PRAVAH unless a later chapter says so. Bibliographic details were checked against OpenAlex/arXiv (see references.bib); the descriptions below come from docs/research/literature-map.md and docs/research/green-2006-reading-notes.md.
Green’s Rice University master’s thesis (Green 2006) is the methodological root of PRAVAH.
What it does.
What it does not do.
How PRAVAH adapts it. The unknowns become K non-negative source strengths with known footprints; G stacks per-source responses over sensors and hours; we use a Bayesian D-criterion log det(I + a_ref² GᵀR⁻¹G) so that singular designs remain comparable; and the decisive score is not the confidence ellipse but held-out forecast error. Every 2-D source-strength extension is a PRAVAH adaptation, not a reproduction. The thesis PDF is a scan without extractable text, so the page pointers above come from the reading notes and should be checked against the original.

title: 1  Background and starting literature
text:
Estimates unknown parameters of a dynamical system obtained by spatially discretising a parameterised transport PDE (finite elements), from sensor readings (reading notes, PDF pp. 17–29).
Uses weighted least squares; for Gaussian noise with covariance R and sensitivity G = ∂y/∂θ the local Fisher information is M(S) = GᵀR⁻¹G, and readings at independent times add information. With M nonsingular, M⁻¹ approximates the estimator covariance (Appendix A, PDF pp. 56–59).
Chooses sensor locations in advance with optimal-design criteria: D-optimality (maximise log det M, i.e. minimise the volume of the confidence ellipsoid), A-optimality (minimise trace M⁻¹) and E-type criteria; it also formulates a weighted approximate design over discrete candidate locations (PDF pp. 34–46).
Illustrates this on a 1-D time-dependent advection–diffusion problem with two unknowns, diffusivity and advection coefficient. Optimised sensors land near x ≈ 0.025 and 0.975 on [0, 1]; the 95 % confidence-ellipse area is ~1.91e-3 (centre placement), ~4.66e-4 (equal spacing) and ~2.97e-4 (optimised), i.e. ~36 % below equal spacing (PDF p. 54).



It does not recover a concentration field or many unknown source strengths; it identifies a handful of transport parameters.
It does not treat low-cost sensor noise, correlated errors, held-out meteorology, or forecasting.
The boundary-sensor result is specific to that PDE, parameter vector and noise model; it is not a rule for placing pollution sensors.
Its asymptotic Fisher confidence regions assume a correctly specified model; under wind or source misspecification their coverage may be poor (PRAVAH gate-04 found exactly this kind of miscalibration when the noise model is wrong).

title: 1  Background and starting literature
section: 1.2 Related work and how each paper is used
text:
1.2 Related work and how each paper is used
Transport models and footprints.

Pennington et al. (2024) build and evaluate a CMAQ chemistry-transport framework for Los Angeles with source apportionment. It is a reference point for what a full 3-D chemical model includes that our passive tracer omits (E01, later E13/E17).
Schlutow et al. (2026) present BLDFM, a fast Eulerian steady-state advection–diffusion solver for concentration and flux footprints. It motivates the footprint view of E04; its code is non-commercially licensed and is not copied.

Source reconstruction and identifiability.

Mons et al. (2017) reconstruct urban pollutant release characteristics by data assimilation. It is the closest analogue to the E03 inverse and to the wind-mismatch experiments planned for plan 3.
Bhardwaj and Subramanian (2026) (arXiv preprint, not peer reviewed) study identifiability-aware source apportionment in city-scale advection–diffusion systems. It shaped the protocol’s separation of identifiability from prediction accuracy (E00, E04, E05). We cite it as a preprint only.

Sensor placement.

Manohar et al. (2018) introduce data-driven sparse placement by POD modes and QR pivoting; Silva et al. (2021) and Karnik et al. (2026) provide the PySensors implementation. PRAVAH’s podqr design follows this, and its QR pivots were checked against PySensors 0.4.3 (E06).
Zhou et al. (2022) apply POD-based planning to PM2.5 monitoring sites across China, with sensor-count and mode-count ablations (relevant to E06 and E08).
Mano et al. (2022) solve air-pollution sensor location–allocation with information theory; Krause et al. (2008) give near-optimal mutual-information placement for Gaussian processes with submodularity guarantees. Both inform the information criteria in E06/E07 and robust placement (E15). Note that the greedy guarantees need not hold with a binding spacing constraint (gate-06).
Choi and Hummel (2025) place low-cost PM2.5 sensors by value of information with multimodal data fusion. It is the closest low-cost-network analogue to PRAVAH’s question (E07, E11, E15). (The literature map lists it as 2026; the publisher record gives 2025.)
Bartos and Kerkez (2021) use observability-based placement for contaminant tracing in river networks: the control-theoretic view behind E04/E05 (observability over time) and E11.

Sequential estimation (plan 2 E09–E11).

Roy et al. (2018) combine a kriged Kalman filter with sparsity-enforcing placement.
Zheng et al. (2009) update the state and parameters of an atmospheric dispersion model online with an ensemble Kalman filter (listed as enkf2009 in the literature map).
Sharma et al. (2019) estimate contaminant distributions from sparse sensors with a Perron–Frobenius operator and EnKF.
Cheng and Paley (2022) estimate a 2-D advection–diffusion process with mobile sensors and optimal guidance.
Raanes et al. (2024) (DAPPER) is the planned reference implementation for data-assimilation cross-checks.

Meteorological uncertainty (plan 3).

Webster and Thomson (2022) treat meteorological uncertainty in Bayesian volcanic-ash inversion with ensemble meteorology: the template for E12 (wind mismatch) and E14 (calibration).
Mues et al. (2018) simulate meteorology and black carbon in the Kathmandu Valley with WRF/WRF-Chem: context for the optional regional case (E17).

Not cited. The literature map also lists a gradient-based mutual-information placement repository (Patel et al., 2026, GitHub only); it has no verifiable bibliographic record and is treated as unverified. Data products (ERA5, FIRMS, WorldPop) concern the optional regional case and are not used in this report.

title: 1  Background and starting literature
text:
1.3 The gap PRAVAH addresses
Placement studies usually score a design on the same information criterion that chose it, or on in-sample reconstruction. PRAVAH asks whether a design chosen from training winds still helps on held-out winds, with noisy sensors and several unknown sources, judged by a forecast endpoint fixed before the data were seen.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1 Protocol in one page
Sources: docs/research/preregistered-protocol.md (approved baseline, 2026-11-12), docs/research/pde-and-discretization.md, docs/research/cross-objective-design.md, the decision files in state/decisions/, and configs/benchmark-v1.yaml.
The protocol (E00) fixes, before any test-period computation, the model, noise, factors, calendar split, held-out winds, one primary endpoint and the success/stop rules. The user approved it on 2026-11-12 as an amendable baseline: if a setting proves numerically infeasible it is amended with a decision file, never silently changed; changes to the primary endpoint or confirmatory claim go to the user. Confirmatory claims start with experiments designed after approval (E07 onward); E02–E06 are exploratory.
Primary endpoint. Held-out, pre-assimilation, one-hour-ahead field-forecast RMSE over all grid cells and test issue times (first 6 h excluded), against the noise-free truth. Primary hypothesis: an optimised network of N ≥ 8 sensors reduces this RMSE relative to random placement by at least 10 %; supported if the 95 % paired-bootstrap CI is above 10 % in ≥ 70 % of N ≥ 8 cells, contradicted if below in ≥ 70 %, otherwise unresolved (including cells not run). Secondary endpoints: source RMSE, post-analysis field RMSE, calibration, synthetic population-weighted error.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.2 Forward model and numerics
The PDE is
\[\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} + \mathbf u(t)\cdot\nabla c = \nabla\cdot(K\nabla c) - \lambda\,(c - c_{bg}) + S(x,y,t),\qquad S = \frac{1}{H}\sum_k a_k\,\phi_k(x,y),\]
solved with FiPy finite volumes. Diffusion and removal are implicit (backward Euler).

Original scheme (protocol §3): implicit first-order upwind advection, dt = 300 s. Verified at first order with mass conserved to ~1e-14 (E01), and kept for all 32² smoke work.
Amendment A2 (2026-11-12): at 64² upwind’s effective diffusivity is 350–2900 m² s⁻¹ against the physical 50, and it fails the dt-halving gate at every dt. FiPy’s VanLeer term is explicit and, unsplit, anti-diffusive across oblique winds (missing cross term). PRAVAH therefore applies VanLeer dimensionally split (x advection, then y advection with diffusion, removal and source) at dt = 30 s. Result: K_eff 49.7–50.9, order ≈ 2, dt-halving change 0.54–0.71 % (gate ≤ 1 %), mass to 1e-15, no negative values; cost ≈ 17× upwind. The limiter makes the scheme ~1 % non-linear, so per-source responses carry a small superposition error (see E07 for its measured impact). Evidence: docs/research/gates/b3-advection-scheme.md, state/decisions/2026-11-12-advection-scheme.md.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.3 Benchmark
pravah.benchmarks generates truth, sensor readings and split manifests deterministically from seeds, with a leakage guard: placement and tuning code cannot read test-period data, evaluation cannot read non-test data, and inference views never contain truth fields (E02: 65 checks). Truth and sensor noise are shared across designs, so all comparisons are paired.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.4 Linear source–receptor operator
Because the PDE is linear in the sources (exactly for upwind, to ~1 % for split VanLeer), readings are
\[y = c_{bg} + G\,a + \varepsilon,\]
where column k of G is the response at the chosen sensors and hours to a unit source k, built from the same solver, winds and spin-up as the truth (a perfect model). Rows stack sensors × hours of the estimator window.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.5 Estimators

NNLS (E03): weighted non-negative least squares on whitened G, optionally with a fixed ridge and a background nuisance.
MAP / ridge (E05, E07 primary): â = argmin ‖(y − c_bg − Ga)/σ‖² + ‖a/a_ref‖², a Gaussian prior with sd a_ref, over a window ending at the issue time (24 h in E07). E07’s secondary NNLS was within ~0.05 of MAP in the pilot.
Forecast (E07): ĉ(t+1) = c_bg + Σ_k â_k(t) F_k(t+1) with F_k the full-grid unit response under the known wind. This is a static-inverse forecast, not a filter (that is E09).

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.6 Fisher information and practical rank
With whitened responses A = a_ref·G/σ the Bayesian D-criterion is log det(I + AᵀA) (Green’s D-optimality plus a prior, so singular designs are comparable); A-criterion trace((I + AᵀA)⁻¹). Floating-point rank uses relative tolerance 1e-8. Because floating-point rank says nothing about noise, we use practical rank = the number of singular values s of G/σ with s·a_ref ≥ 1, i.e. the number of source combinations that a reference-sized change moves by at least one noise σ. This threshold was not preregistered and is lenient: gate-05 noted that practical rank ≥ 1 still allows ~100 % error per mode.

2.8 Evaluation contract

Designs use training data only; estimators use observations up to the issue time only; truth is read only by the scorer.
Test-period values are computed once per frozen configuration; a re-run after a change is an amendment.
Failures (undefined designs, non-identifiable cases, all-zero estimates) are counted, never dropped.
Each run records command, git revision, seeds, configuration, environment and job ID (reports/runs/runs.jsonl).
Every experiment gets an independent audit by a separate agent (docs/research/gates/). The auditors are the same model family as the authors, so independence is by task and re-derivation, not by a different reviewer.

title: 6  E03 Static source-strength inverse (known wind)
text:
6.1 Design
Question. With fixed (non-optimised) sensors, known wind and a perfect model, can a weighted non-negative inverse recover source strengths? Evidence label: exploratory; a negative result. Current status: rerun at a_ref = 1 g s⁻¹ (A1); the tables below are from that rerun (commit 04bbd28).
Headline. The weighted sensitivity matrix is rank-deficient (tolerance 1e-8) in all 648 fits, at both the old and the new source scale. Rank does not depend on scale, so the cause is structural: ≤ 8 fixed sensors and a 24 h window cannot separate the sources. For K = 2, two of three seeds put every sensor outside the plumes. The lever is sensor placement (E06/E07) and wind change (E05), not the estimator.
Simulated passive tracer only; nothing here is evidence about ambient PM2.5. Every number below is generated from tables/e03-inversion.csv, tables/e03-estimates.csv, tables/e03-validity.csv and tables/e03-nonidentifiable.json, written by scripts/e03_inversion.py (one registered run) and rendered by tables/make_e03_md.py.

title: 6  E03 Static source-strength inverse (known wind)
text:
Perfect model: the response matrix is built from the same transient solver, winds and spin-up as the hidden truth, so this measures the inverse problem only, not model mismatch. Source locations and shapes are known; the unknowns are the source strengths (nonnegative) and, in one arm, a constant background.
Smoke scale (32² grid, 12 h spin-up, one 24 h window of hourly readings), not the preregistered 64² / 60-day design. Three replicate seeds per cell; each seed has its own truth and its own noise stream.
Sources K ∈ {2, 4, 8}, sensors ∈ {2, 4, 8} chosen by a fixed deterministic rule from the admissible candidate sites (not optimised).
Noise levels. Three data-relative levels set σ₀ to a fixed fraction r of the rms noise-free anomaly at the chosen sensors, with per-site σ varying by a factor up to 9 (heteroscedastic, so weighting is not a no-op). A fourth level is the preregistered homoscedastic noise (5% of the median background-dominated truth), read through the leak-checked inference view; there weighting and no weighting are mathematically identical.
Estimators: unweighted NNLS, noise-weighted NNLS, noise-weighted ridge NNLS (one fixed relative ridge, chosen before any run, not tuned); each with the background known (subtracted) or estimated as a sign-free nuisance coefficient.
Scores: source relative RMSE (‖â − a‖/‖a‖), field RMSE over the whole grid and window against the noise-free truth anomaly (compared with the RMSE of the all-zero estimate), measurement fit (rms of residual over true σ; about 1 when the model and noise are consistent), and identifiability diagnostics (rank and conditioning of the weighted sensitivity matrix at relative tolerance 1e-8, and the fraction of sources whose local Cramér–Rao standard deviation is at most half the true strength). The CRB is an unconstrained local approximation. No pass/fail threshold on error was preregistered for this experiment, so none is applied; outcomes are described, not graded.

title: 6  E03 Static source-strength inverse (known wind)
text:
6.7 Limitations

Smoke scale and perfect model only: no wind, diffusivity, removal or location error, single noise realisation per cell, three seeds, deterministic non-optimised sensor sites. No claim about generality or about the preregistered 64² design.
The tables use the amended source scale a_ref = 1 g s⁻¹ (A1), chosen after seeing data, so they are exploratory. The data-relative noise levels are chosen so the signal is visible; they are not the preregistered noise, which is reported separately. (Earlier text here describing the preregistered 100 µg s⁻¹ scale is superseded.)
The estimate is scored in-window on the analysis field, not as a held-out forecast, so it is not the primary endpoint.
Rank decisions depend on the 1e-8 relative tolerance; badly conditioned but nominally full-rank cells are not identifiable in practice, which the conditioning column shows.
The ridge strength is a single fixed value; no validation-based selection was run.
Sources whose plume barely reaches any chosen sensor give near-zero columns of the sensitivity matrix; unregularised NNLS can then assign them enormous strengths for negligible change in the readings. Errors many orders above 1 are this numerical effect, reported as observed and not clipped. The fixed, non-optimised sensor rule and 24 h window may be a main cause; sensor placement is a later experiment and was not varied here.
The run budget for this experiment was used up, so no redesign (different window, tolerance or sensor rule) was run after seeing these results.
Findings from these runs stay preliminary.

title: 6  E03 Static source-strength inverse (known wind)
text:
6.8 Audit outcome (gate-03)
Gate-03 found the code engineering-sound (23 tests pass) but did not clear the baseline for fair placement comparisons: no fit is full rank, so the estimator has no demonstrated recovery regime. It recommended a regime where rank = K is achievable (longer window, optimised sensors or larger source scale), a noise-referenced rank criterion, and validation-only ridge tuning. What changed: the source scale (A1), the noise-referenced practical rank used from E04 on, a prior-referenced ridge (MAP) in E05/E07, and optimised placement (E06/E07). The “identifiable recovery” half of the E03 hypothesis remains untested in this configuration.

title: 7  E04 Footprints, Fisher information and identifiability
text:
7.1 Design
Question. Which source combinations can a sensor network actually distinguish, and does the singular spectrum of the stacked response predict this better than sensor count or coverage? Evidence label: exploratory (one scenario layout, one replicate). Current status: rerun at a_ref = 1 g s⁻¹ (A1, commit 04bbd28).
Headline. At the preregistered σ (0.253 µg m⁻³) the greedy D-optimal (“informative”) 4-sensor design reaches practical rank 4/4 under both winds; the coverage design 1 (westerly) or 2 (veering); the redundant design 2. Moving the source vector along the weakest mode changes the data by less than 1σ in 9 of 12 cases, all for non-informative designs. At the old 100 µg s⁻¹ scale the practical rank was 0/4 for every design (superseded).
Simulated passive tracer only; nothing here is evidence about ambient PM2.5. Every number below is generated by scripts/e04_footprints.py (one registered run) into tables/e04-identifiability.csv, tables/e04-identifiability.md and tables/e04-results.md; the figure is figures/e04-footprints.png. Settings are in tables/e04-meta.json.

title: 7  E04 Footprints, Fisher information and identifiability
text:
Smoke scale (32² grid, 12 h spin-up, 24 h window), perfect model, known source locations (four sources), two training wind regimes (steady westerly, veering). G is built from the truth’s own solver; no estimator sees the truth strengths except the counterexample below, where they define the “true vector”.
Three 4-sensor designs, chosen from G and the admissible sites only: informative (greedy Bayesian D-optimal, prior sd equal to the reference rate), redundant (the four admissible sites nearest the first informative site that respect the minimum separation) and coverage (farthest-point spreading). Designs are chosen under the first wind and evaluated under both.
Practical rank: the number of singular values s of G/σ with s·A_ref ≥ 1, i.e. the modes in which a reference-sized source change moves the data by at least one noise σ. This is our operationalisation of “rank at the preregistered noise scale”; it is not a preregistered threshold. Floating-point rank (relative tolerance 1e-8) is reported beside it.
Noise scales: the preregistered σ, and an extra non-preregistered “information scale” σ (0.1 × rms reference signal over admissible sites). It was added when, at the old 100 µg s⁻¹ scale, no mode was above noise; it is a rescaling, not a realistic instrument.
Counterexample: the true strength vector is moved along the weakest right singular vector of G/σ (nonnegativity kept, step at most half of ‖a‖). If the data change is below one σ, the two vectors fit equally well yet differ.
Ellipses are local 95% ellipses of the posterior covariance (Fisher plus a prior of sd A_ref), because the unregularised Fisher matrix is singular in several cases.

7.3 Audit outcome (gate-04)
Gate-04 partly cleared E04. The Fisher/CRB machinery is correct in the linear-Gaussian interior case and conservative under the NNLS constraint, but badly miscalibrated when the noise model is wrong, and it cannot be evaluated for designs whose Fisher matrix is singular. The hypothesis (spectrum beats count or coverage) remained unresolved: one replicate, at the time at a scale where nothing was above noise. It also noted that the 1e-8 rank rule is applied to singular values in one place and eigenvalues in another. What changed: A1 rescaled the problem, the Bayesian (prior-regularised) D-criterion is used so singular designs stay comparable, and the paired-seed comparison moved to E06/E07.

title: 8  E05 Temporal observability: sensor count versus observation window
text:
32² grid, 12 h spin-up, perfect model, known source locations and winds, ideal white sensors, 20 seeds (each seed changes sources, strengths, random nested sensor sites and noise draws; noise draws are identical across winds).
Sensors N ∈ {2, 4, 8} (random, nested, never optimised); sources K ∈ {2, 4}; window W ∈ {1, 6, 24, 168} h ending at the issue hour; readings per sensor m ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} spread over W (m = 1 is the reading at the issue hour; m > W is not run).
Winds: constant = exactly 3 m s⁻¹ from 270° (null control); drifting = the benchmark’s steady westerly, whose direction is re-drawn N(270°, 10°) every 48 h; changing = veering 270° → 315° during the first 12 h of each 48 h block. Drifting and changing share speed factors.

title: 8  E05 Temporal observability: sensor count versus observation window
text:
8.4 Interpretation (kept separate from the observations)
The hypothesis is that changing wind directions raise effective rank for constant sources, while repeated readings under the same transport only reduce noise. Read the window-gain table first: the constant-wind row isolates elapsed time, and the difference-in-differences rows isolate wind change. A gain under constant wind would contradict the second half of the hypothesis; a positive DiD supports the first. The equal-readings and matched-budget tables address the sensor-savings question without letting reading count stand in for window length. Practical rank ≥ 1 still allows roughly 100 % error per mode, so the median error columns matter as much as the rank columns.

8.5 Audit outcome (gate-05)
Gate-05: the computation is valid and reproduces bit-for-bit, the look-ahead guard and seed pairing are correct, but the v1 chapter was not cleared for interpretation (see the warning box). What changed in v2: an exactly constant wind as a null control, the drifting wind as a separate level, a prior-based ridge (sd a_ref) to stop blow-ups, medians instead of means, a fixed m = 4, seed as the unit with bootstrap and sign tests, and an equal-readings comparison. The audit judged the hypothesis unresolved with a positive exploratory signal for “wind change, not elapsed time, adds rank”; v2 strengthens that signal but stays exploratory because the contrasts were chosen after the audit.

title: 9  E06 Placement algorithms and their own objectives
text:
Smoke scale (32² grid, 12 h spin-up, 4 training days), perfect model, ideal white sensors. Winds: steady westerly and veering (training regime). Two seeds × K ∈ {2, 4} sources from the benchmark draw. Budgets k ∈ {2, 4, 8}.
Scale: a_ref from amendment A1 (1 g/s), σ = each scenario’s preregistered noise sd.
Design inputs (training split only): sensitivities G over all 96 training hours (known source locations, the truth’s solver and winds); POD snapshots = noise-free field at all sites over the 96 training hours. Validation-split fields are used only to score field reconstruction; the test split is not read.
Two candidate sets: full = all admissible lattice sites (the 1250 m minimum spacing binds); small = admissible sites on every third lattice node (≤ 25 candidates, 1875 m apart, spacing never binds), where exhaustive search over all feasible k-subsets gives the gap of each greedy design to the optimum of its own objective.
Designs: uniform, random, coverage, source_near (baselines); dopt and aopt (greedy Bayesian D/A, prior sd a_ref); diversity (footprint coherence with an SNR ≥ 1 eligibility rule); podqr (POD/QR with the noise-aware mode count r_eff); podqr_num (exploratory, noise-unaware: numerical mode count).
Practical rank: number of singular values s of G_S/σ with s·a_ref ≥ 1, over the 96 h training window.

title: 9  E06 Placement algorithms and their own objectives
text:
9.3 Interpretation
Read against the tables above (qualitative statements only; the numbers are in the generated fragments):

Own goals. Greedy D-opt matched the exhaustive optimum of its objective on the small set and had the largest D value of all designs on the full set in every case. Greedy A-opt was close to its exhaustive optimum on the small set but on the full set D-opt designs usually had an equal or slightly larger A value, which is possible because A is not submodular and greedy A has no guarantee. Footprint diversity often missed the minimum coherence by a noticeable margin: its lexicographic greedy rule is a heuristic for that goal. Unconstrained QR pivots matched scipy and PySensors (tests); on the small set the exploratory noise-unaware variant reached the optimum of the log-det objective in some cases and not others.
POD/QR at this noise level. At the preregistered σ the time-varying part of the 4-day training field has at most a couple of above-noise modes (often none), so the noise-aware POD/QR design is undefined for almost every budget. This is a property of the smoke calendar (two to four piecewise-steady wind blocks, constant sources), not of POD/QR in general; the same reason makes the field-reconstruction score uninformative (equal to the training-mean baseline) for almost every design. The exploratory noise-unaware variant places sensors that serve a basis made partly of sub-noise structure.
Cross-criterion trade-offs. Source-informed designs (D, A, diversity, source_near) reached full practical rank at small budgets far more often than the uniform, random and coverage baselines, which use no source information. This is in-sample (scored on the same 96 training hours the designs optimise) and mostly reflects knowing the source locations: the locations-only source_near design ties D-opt in 21 of 24 cases (gate-06). It agrees with E04 at a_ref = 1 g/s, where the greedy D-opt design also reached 4/4; practical rank was 0 everywhere only at the old 100 µg/s scale. The D/A designs are not low-coherence designs, and the low-coherence designs give up D value: the objectives pick different networks. Nothing here says which network is better for source, field or forecast error; that is E07’s question.

title: 9  E06 Placement algorithms and their own objectives
text:
9.4 Audit outcome (gate-06)
Gate-06 cleared E06 as a methods/reproduction step: every strategy sees the same candidates, budget and spacing; the Bayesian D/A/E formulas and scaling are right; tie-breaking is deterministic; QR pivots match PySensors 0.4.3; the committed CSV reproduces bit-for-bit (108/108 rows on two re-run scenarios). It set three conditions before E07:

Declare what each design knows. “Training-only” meant training hours, not training information: sources are constant, so the noise-free POD archive contains the true strengths. The source-informed designs also know the true source locations; the locations-only source_near ties D-opt in 21 of 24 cases, so most of the advantage is knowing where the sources are.
Score on held-out hours, with an AR(1) noise arm and per-site σ (in-sample practical rank flatters designs; in one spot case A-opt and diversity dropped from 4 to 3 on held-out hours).
Fix the POD mode-count rule in advance and check greedy optimality where spacing binds: on a synthetic 5 × 5 lattice with binding spacing greedy D was exact in only 35/80 cases (max relative gap 19.8 %), whereas the small candidate set used above never binds.

All three were built into the E07 design note before any E07 computation.

9.5 Limitations
Smoke scale, 8 scenarios, a 96 h design window that is also the POD training window, a perfect model and noise-free POD archives. The small candidate set never makes the spacing rule bind, so the exhaustive gaps say nothing about greedy behaviour under binding spacing. The POD results are dominated by the short, piecewise-steady training calendar (few above-noise modes) and should not be read as a property of POD/QR in general. No design was evaluated on a held-out inference task; that is E07.

source_near beats dopt in 115/120 paired (scenario, k) comparisons with white noise (110 with AR(1), 118 with per-site σ), in all 20 source layouts, by a median relative margin of ≈ 0.4 (gate-07: IQR 0.23–0.60; bootstrap CI over layouts 0.28–0.56). 10.4.2 Mechanism: per-window rank loss under an unseen wind
Field checks on two scenarios (gate-07, veering:2:7 and mixed:4:9):

dopt networks have no rank-deficient 24 h windows during training but 17.6 % in the test period; all 75 deficient windows fall in the held-out steady southerly blocks — a direction never seen in training. source_near has none.
Those windows carry 97.5 % (veering:2:7) and 37 % (mixed:4:9) of dopt’s squared forecast error.
Sweep-wide (table above), dopt has at least one deficient test window in 30/40 scenarios at k = 8 against 7/40 for source_near.
Whole-period information criteria miss this: D on the test winds favours source_near in only 35/120 cases, and selecting by D_test still costs a median forecast regret of 0.37.

Reading (inference): designs tuned to the training winds do not transfer to an unseen wind direction, while sensors at the sources stay informative whatever the wind. The evidence rests on one unseen direction, and the window analysis covers 2 scenarios in detail.


10.4.3 Endpoint agreement is close to built in
The network best on forecast is also best on source, analysis and population-weighted error (forecast-best equals source-best in 116/120; median off-diagonal regret 0). But all four endpoints are functions of the same static estimate under a perfect model and constant sources, so agreement is expected; it is weak evidence about the plan’s “no single network wins” hypothesis and must not be stated as a general finding.


10.4.4 Other checks

Leakage: designs rebuilt with every non-training hour set to NaN give the committed sites; forecast scores were reproduced to 5 digits by an independent implementation.
VanLeer superposition (A2): the max superposition error over the full calendar is a median 0.038 µg m⁻³ and 0.183 at worst (0.73σ at a single cell-hour), ~27× the 96 h figure quoted in A2; re-scoring on a perfectly linear truth changed RMSE by ≤ 1e-4 and kept the ordering.
Greedy optimality: greedy + swap is exact in 146/160 block checks (greedy alone 91/160); hotspot has higher D_train than dopt in 10/120 cases. This does not affect the comparison (source_near never has the highest D_train).
podqr was undefined in 1 (k = 8) and 3 (k = 16) of 40 scenarios per arm — fewer than the design note predicted.

Span and sensor count beat reading density. For random networks at K = 4, k = 8, nRMSE is 0.46 for a snapshot, 0.23 over 24 h and 0.10 over 168 h. At equal total readings, 4k sensors × 6 readings beat k × 24 in 11 of 12 scenarios.
H2 reversed in the pilot. Near-source is more noise-sensitive in relative terms, though far better in absolute terms. The preregistered test is unchanged.
H3 is inconclusive. H5 (near-source beats D-optimal): 10 of 12 scenarios at k = 8.







WarningEstimator-memory caveat (gate-09)



E08 uses windowed estimators (windows of 1–168 h). Gate-09 showed that strategy orderings flip between short and unlimited estimator memory (see the E07 and E09 chapters). E08’s strategy comparisons, H5 especially, therefore hold for windowed estimators only. The all-past-data rerun above confirms this: H5 reverses.

title: 12  E09 Causal sequential filtering
text:
Hour-to-hour transition: the linear operator of the FiPy upwind step, recovered by probing the solver and checked against fresh probes.
Field-only filter (kf_field): corrects the concentration field only.
Augmented filter (kf_aug): estimates the field and the constant source strengths jointly.
AR(1) variant (kf_aug_ar1): adds sensor-error states for correlated noise.
Baselines: E07’s frozen 24 h-window MAP (map24), the open-loop model, persistence and climatology.
Tests: against independent references (a scalar case, equivalence with the batch posterior, causality, missing sensors, NEES and NIS on a perfect-model Monte Carlo).

title: 12  E09 Causal sequential filtering
text:
12.2 Results






Figure 12.1: E09: forecast error over the test period for each estimator and design.




Memory is what matters. With a perfect model, kf_aug is exactly the batch MAP over all past data. It cuts 1-hour forecast error by a median 58–74 % against map24 (10–12 of 12 scenarios per design), and by 77–91 % at 24 h. Gate-09’s 2×2 control attributes a median 0.99 of the log-RMSE gain to using all past data. The prior adds essentially nothing.
Correcting the field alone is almost useless. kf_field beats open loop only at 1 h and is 1.6–13× worse than map24. Corrections leave a 10 km domain with the wind within hours, so forecast skill comes from estimating the persistent sources.
Calibration:

Under white noise, kf_aug is calibrated: 50/80/95 % coverage of 0.50/0.82/0.97. At 64² with all past data, 95 % coverage is 0.95.
Under AR(1) noise it is overconfident: 95 % coverage 0.48. The usual NIS check misses this; lag-1 innovation autocorrelation (0.80) catches it.
Modelling the correlated noise (kf_aug_ar1) restores calibration (0.945) and beats map24 in 12 of 12 scenarios.

Consequence for placement (64²): with all past data, D-optimal beats near-source in 103/120 E07 pairs, reversing E07’s 24 h-window ordering (see the E07 chapter).

title: 12  E09 Causal sequential filtering
text:
12.3 Limits and what carries forward

32² only, with the upwind operator. VanLeer, the 64² scheme, is non-linear and has no exact Kalman operator.
At 64², the planned baseline is the growing-window MAP on cached unit responses, which is equivalent to kf_aug. An ensemble filter is used only where process noise or model error is needed.
E10 reuses the augmented filter; E11 reuses the causal scorer. Because the covariance recursion does not depend on data, a design’s forecast-variance trace can be computed before any data exists, which gives a training-only forecast-placement objective.
Estimator memory, or assumed source persistence, is a declared factor in E10 and E11.

15.2 Results






Note“Persistence” here is an oracle bound (gate-12-17)



The persistence baseline carries the true field at hour t to t + 1 in every grid cell. No sensor network can do that, so “worse than persistence” means worse than an unreachable bound, not worse than a naive forecast.








Figure 15.1: E12: source-strength bias and forecast skill under each wind error.




Forecast skill collapses quickly. Direction errors of 30° or more, a lag of 2 h or more, and AR(1) noise with sd 30° all make the 1 h forecast worse than persistence (0/6 clusters). A +10° error is about level with persistence. Underestimating the speed keeps skill (6/6).
Source–transport compensation.

Source RMSE rises 1.6–16×.
The fit stays near perfect (ratio 1.01–1.33) only for speed errors, +10° and AR 15°: that is where compensation is deceptive. For a 30° direction error, a lag or AR 30°, the fit ratio rises to 1.6–4.3 and does warn.
Speed errors bias the strengths low (−15 % for × 0.8, −32 % for × 0.6).
95 % coverage of the strengths collapses to 0.00–0.54.
The fit looks good while the answer is wrong: 298 “deceptive fit” cells.

Warning sign. Lag-1 innovation autocorrelation rises to 0.13–0.89. It stays weak for speed × 0.8.
Memory. The large gain from using all past data (+0.6 to +0.77 with the true wind) mostly vanishes under any wind error.
Placement. Under the wrong wind, D-optimal and near-source are within a few per cent of each other. Rankings built on ratios flip with memory, but that is an artefact of the denominator.

The persistence baseline carries the true field at hour t to t + 1 in every grid cell. No sensor network can do that, so “worse than persistence” means worse than an unreachable bound, not worse than a naive forecast.








Figure 16.1: E13: uncertainty coverage and forecast skill under each mismatch.




A wrong background is fixable. A +1 µg/m³ offset (4σ) destroys forecasts (skill vs persistence −3.5), biases the sources by +128 % and gives zero coverage. Estimating the background repairs this fully (skill +0.94, coverage 0.96, 6/6). A drifting background is only partly repaired.
Silent failure. At the sensors, a background offset and a bias common to all sensors look identical.

The background term fixes the offset but makes the common bias worse (skill −3.9).
Every diagnostic looks perfect: fit ratio 1.00, white innovations, coverage 0.96. Yet forecasts are far worse than persistence.
Telling the two apart needs outside information, such as a reference instrument or an upwind background site.

Wrong source assumptions are not fixable. For a shifted source, a wider footprint or a missing source, no estimator beats persistence at k = 8. A shifted source does show in the residuals (fit ratio 1.3–3.5, lag-1 0.30–0.82). A wide footprint or a missing source barely does (fit ratio 1.12–1.27).
Sensor errors.

AR(1) noise leaves strengths unbiased, but coverage falls to 0.45–0.60. Lag-1 autocorrelation warns (0.78).
Random outages are benign, even at 50 % missing.
Per-site bias destroys coverage.
Under drift, all past data helps (+0.57 vs the 24 h window, 6/6).

Diagnostics: eight truth-free diagnostics, each computed from the data before each 24 h block. Tests confirm they are unchanged when all truth is replaced by NaN.

L2: 90 % coverage is below 0.70.

title: 17  E14 Reliability diagnostics
text:
17.2 Results






Note“Persistence” here is an oracle bound (gate-12-17)



The persistence baseline carries the true field at hour t to t + 1 in every grid cell. No sensor network can do that, so “worse than persistence” means worse than an unreachable bound, not worse than a naive forecast.








Figure 17.1: E14: how well each diagnostic separates reliable from unreliable blocks (ROC).









Figure 17.2: E14: interval coverage with the true and with a wrong wind.




Early warning works only moderately. The best warning of forecast failure is the sensor skill over the previous day, with AUC 0.71 [0.64, 0.77]. It reaches 0.81–0.86 for large direction or timing errors. Spread, fit and NIS give 0.65–0.67. For coverage failure, the best AUC is 0.63–0.65.
Calibration depends on the wind. With the true wind, 90 % coverage is 0.91–0.995, but 50 % coverage is only 0.44–0.47. With a wrong wind it collapses: 0.07 for a 30° direction error.
Failures nobody flags.

A speed error of × 0.8 is undetectable (AUC 0.46–0.57).
An omitted source is unflagged only for random networks. For D-optimal and near-source networks it shows clearly (NIS ≈ 4, lag-1 0.41, AUC 0.84–0.89). Those networks were, however, designed knowing the omitted source.
NIS misses AR(1) noise. Lag-1 autocorrelation detects it (0.63 vs −0.03), but as a warning of forecast failure it is weak (AUC 0.58).

title: 17  E14 Reliability diagnostics
text:
17.3 Limits

The 6 clusters are dependent.
The within-config AUC was chosen after seeing results. It lowers the best score (0.74 to 0.71) rather than flattering it.
Together with E13’s silent failure, these results mean that truth-free checks cannot certify a map. They can only flag some failures.

Placement still matters with the true wind. D-optimal and near-source beat random in every case (20 of 20 clusters at k = 8), by 35–50 % under the 24 h window and 53–64 % with all past data.
The D-optimal vs near-source ordering mostly disappears.

The two tie in the cool season.
In the unseen monsoon regime, near-source edges ahead under the 24 h window (16 of 20). This is E07’s direction, much weaker, and it does not survive Holm correction over the 18 such tests.
With all past data they tie. E07/E08’s clear D-optimal win does not appear under these calm, rotating winds.

Only memory beats the persistence bound. Persistence here carries the true field forward one hour, which no network can do. The 24 h-window forecasts are 1.2–1.4× its error, beating it in only 3–5 of 20 clusters. All-past-data forecasts beat it by about 10×.
The wrong wind cancels both advantages. The ERA5 point nearest Belauri differs from the box mean by about 17° and 13 % in speed (a 40 % vector error). Using it instead of the box mean puts every forecast at 1.8–3.7× the persistence bound (still 0.43–0.76× the background-only error). All strategies become nearly equal and the memory gain disappears. This is a transport floor: forecasts using the true source strengths with the wrong wind are just as bad (0.047 vs 0.0465), so better estimation cannot fix it. This reproduces E12 under realistic winds.

Uniform wind. The ERA5 wind varies inside the box by about as much as its mean, so a spatially varying wind is the main missing ingredient.

Mixing depth. The cool-season boundary layer (median 47–88 m) is much shallower than the model’s 500 m.
Short calendar. The 20 clusters in each case share one wind history.

title: 21  Lessons and corrections
text:
21.1 What these corrections taught us
Every experiment was audited by a separate agent (“gate”), working from the code, tables and run records rather than the author’s summary. The auditors share the authors’ model family, so their independence comes from the task split and from re-deriving numbers. This chapter collects what they caught and what was done about it. Superseded results stay in Git history and in the journals; they are not deleted.

title: 21  Lessons and corrections
text:
Check the signal-to-noise ratio first. Three experiments were run before the scale problem was acted on; a one-line estimate in the protocol audit had already predicted it.
A “steady” control must be exactly steady. The E05 confound came from a realistic-looking jitter in the control.
Means of ill-posed estimates are meaningless. Use medians, prior-referenced regularisation, and count failures.
Always include a dumb control that knows the same thing. The locations-only control is what revealed that the E06/E07 gains were mostly knowledge of source locations.
In-sample information is not held-out performance. Whole-period D on training (and even on test) winds missed the short windows in which a source became invisible.
Amendments are fine if recorded. Each change above has a decision file or journal entry with its evidence and the results it affects.

title: 22  Next steps
text:
22.5 Open decisions and known gaps

Confirmatory scope of E07 (above).
Whether to make source_near (or a wind-robust variant) the reference design going forward; this is outcome-driven and must be preregistered for E11/E15, not adopted retroactively.
E03 remains rank-deficient for structural reasons; a configuration where the “identifiable recovery” half of its hypothesis can be tested has not been run.
E04’s spectrum-vs-coverage hypothesis has not been tested across seeds; the 1e-8 rank rule is applied on different scales in two code paths (gate-04).
Study-boundary behaviour of both advection schemes has no independent check.
No held-out forecast evaluation outside E07; no wind error or model mismatch anywhere yet.

title: 22  Next steps
text:
22.6 Real data (E17, E18)

E17: a regional case near Belauri, Kanchanpur, using ERA5 reanalysis winds and synthetic emissions. It tests whether the method rankings survive realistic wind sequences. It is not a validation.
E18: not conducted. No usable public PM2.5 monitoring exists near Belauri: two Department of Environment stations lie within 100 km, with short records. See docs/research/observational-validation-audit.md.
